That's when the numbers started decreasing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 80, line 22 of today's transcript, you started talking about the living shield, about the human shield in Kozarac. You mentioned a name that was not recorded. What did you tell us? Who held whom as human shield? Which name did you mention?

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: Based on interviews with people of both genders of Muslim ethnicity as we were looking for the Green Berets and their whereabouts, we received information from several witnesses that members of the Green Berets, among them Sulejman Kosuran, Kole, were against the possibility of using the corridor when people went to Trnopolje. They didn't mention the term "human shield." It was just my conclusion that that's how that human shield was created.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at P7209 next. This document has not been translated. It originates from the Ministry of Interior, that is to say, the public security centre in Prijedor, dated 13th of June, 1992. It contains information on the conduct of members of the special detachment of the CSB in Banja Luka in -- during a previous period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the members of the special detachment of the Banja Luka CSB arrived in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: No. I have information that I obtained only after the war and that I learned was partially incorrect, was that the interrogation centre in Omarska was established by the MUP. When General Talic stated that the command of the 1st Krajina Corps participated in it, it is then only that I learned of that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you hear about Omarska and the army's participation in it?

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: As per official order, the army was supposed to perform guard duty in the outer perimeter about a couple of hundred metres outside the compound and that they were not in contact with those who were inside it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 85, line 15 of today's transcript, it was put to you that throughout the summer of 1992, there were crimes taking place in Keraterm. What is your knowledge about what happened in Keraterm, or what was happening in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: First, I said that during that period we were not allowed inside and that we were constantly arguing with those from the MUP who were in Keraterm. We, as military intelligence, could not obtain information. As for the shooting that took place during the night, I don't remember exactly when, happened immediately after the operation in Carakovo. I heard that there was a lot of firing during the night, and there were only one or two officers on duty at the command who told me that there was firing and movement. Later on, I learned it was an act of retaliation. That is what I know, more or less. If we came in contact with any of the civilians we interrogated who had come from Keraterm, we asked that a medical report be drafted if they showed visible signs of physical violence, but I don't recall if any of the people who had been physically beaten had come to me. And what I can confirm with certainty, that we did not physically beat anyone while interrogating them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could I seek clarification. You've told us several times now that the killing in Keraterm was because of retaliation. Do you know who committed those killings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My knowledge is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't know any first or last names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What makes you so pertinent to tell us so often that it was retaliation without even knowing who committed those killings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that a policeman was killed. His nickname was Krivi, his last name was Curguz, but I don't remember his first name. During the operations in Carakovo. Those are all stories I heard from other people, and there were assumptions made that it happened immediately after he was killed. I don't know if it is correct or not but that's what people talked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that made you believe that it was retaliation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't say I -- I don't say it was retaliation. I just say that I heard that the motive of it was retaliation. It is not my assertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll check that, whether you never said that. Please continue, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is your knowledge? Except for the people from Carakovo, were there any other prisoners in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am not familiar with your markings, 1, 2, 3, or 5. That's not something I ever heard about before. I hear it from you for the first time. The first room, I don't know whether it was called room 1, 2, 3, or 5, housed civilians, or prisoners, that we were supposed to interrogate. I don't know how many there were, though. And they were there even before the operation in Carakovo. That is what I could observe. Their interrogation took place inside Keraterm, and during the initial period I did not have access to Keraterm. Later on when some senior officers intervened and dealt with the issue, I did have access, but it only took place later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In terms of what you could hear, did you learn that only people from Carakovo were killed or all those who were in Keraterm at that moment?

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: According to our information, I don't think fire was opened at other rooms which housed people who were not from Carakovo. Only the one where the Carakovo people were. I don't know anything about any specific numbers though.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. This is all we had for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still one follow-up question to one of my previous questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I understand you well that you assumed that the killing took place shortly after that officer or that soldier was killed, that for that purpose you assumed that it must have been retaliation that led the perpetrators to kill the large number of people in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: In my statements, I tried to say that I only heard about such information. I heard from some people that it was done as retaliation. It is not something I know. I only heard about it. I could only hear others retell the story, saying that it was retaliation for the killing of so-and-so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, a minute ago you said -- well, okay. Let's -- who told you that it was retaliation?

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: A few days after, I attended a briefing of the intelligence department, and I think I heard from someone who was in charge of security say concisely about what had happened that night. They said that it involved civilians brought in from Carakovo and that in all likelihood it concerned retaliation. So that was our knowledge at the time. It's not something I knew about, and I'm not trying to justify it as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You also said that you never told us that -- that it was retaliation.

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: I did say that but I never claimed it was my opinion. I only said that I heard about it being an act of retaliation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, may I remind you that you said today: "I know that it was a case of retaliation," which is not: "I know that someone said that it possibly was or likely was a case of retaliation." You said: "I know that it was a case of retaliation."

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: I think the latter is correct, not the first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: If I did say so, I apologise. It is not my own conclusion that it involved retaliation, and I never wanted to assert that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions, Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Very briefly. Could we have 65 ter 32192.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, this is a criminal report from the public prosecutor's office in Prijedor regarding Mr. Zigic. We see in the fifth line that he's described as "... a member of the unit securing the Keraterm temporary prison in Prijedor ..." Now I'm not suggesting it was only the VRS or that the MUP wasn't involved, but there were soldiers that assisted in securing Keraterm, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: According to the information I have, the answer is no. However, given the fact that I saw Zigic when I passed by, then the answer would be yes. But I don't think he was there on any orders. It is just my opinion. In any case, I wasn't familiar with that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And can we have 65 ter 10855. Page 3 in the English and 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As it comes up, this is part of an interview with Simo Drljaca in Kozarski Vjesnik in 1993. At the top of the fourth column on page 2 in the B/C/S, and just above "many had their own, Muslims and Croats," in the middle of the page in English, we read him say: "The co-operation with the Army of the Serb republic as well as the officers was exceptional. The co-operation occurred in the joint cleansing of renegades on the terrain, joint work at the check-points, joint intervention group for maintaining the public peace and order, as well as in the combat against terrorist groups." What Mr. Drljaca is saying here, that's the truth: Co-operation between the VRS and the MUP in Prijedor was strong and constant, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: Your question was a long one and yet I'm expected to answer concisely. In any case, my answer would be not in entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tendered those two documents, 65 ter 32192 and 10855.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 32192 receives number P7210; and 10855 receives P7211.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7210 and P7211 are admitted into evidence. I have one question for you, Witness, a short one. Further questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In paragraph 28 of your statement, you say that there had been abuse of while belts in Trnopolje camp. Well, you used the word "camp" there. But apart from that, could you tell us what the outcome of the investigation into the abuse of white belts in Trnopolje camp was?

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: It wasn't done by military policemen. It was done by soldiers and citizens who identified themselves as military policemen by obtaining a white belt somewhere. We were against it, and the security organs undertook measures and arrested those who had such belts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give us --

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: As a lawyer, I undertook other measures in order to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that reports or Official Notes were made in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: I suppose those who worked on it made Official Notes, but I did not, since it didn't concern me directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, talking about Official Notes. When you interviewed or when you interrogated persons in the context of your duties, did you make written notes or written reports of those interviews?

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We drafted notes and we informed the assistant commander. And along our direct line of the intelligence and security organ, we informed the corps in our service. So there were two lines of communication in parallel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there must be a whole trace of paperwork in relation to what you did at that time?

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: I suppose it has been preserved somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could you also tell us what measures you said you took against those who abused white belts?

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: Against those who misused white belts, the criminal investigation departments of the police and the security organs dealt with it. We in the intelligence department did not deal with it. What I tried to do, but I was interrupted a couple of times in explaining, was that I sought to be involved as a lawyer in the intelligence department. We asked that the safety of citizens be improved by having military police issue orders -- actually, receipts with numbers and lists of equipment issued to each and every military policemen, so that if we came across such pieces of equipment, we could identify the policeman involved. Having done this, we realised that it did not concern any military policemen and that it was a clearly misuse. As for what was done with such cases subsequently, that is something I don't know. The criminal investigation department was involved in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one question, sir. Paragraph 25 of your statement you say that Muslims were paying to go to Trnopolje. My one question is: Who did they make the payment to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To such citizens who transported them, mostly in vans. They would transport eight people. I mentioned the one who boasted of having earned 4.000 German marks for a number of rounds he did. Some also used their own vehicles. Others were brought there by their family members. So they went voluntarily and were even prepared to pay to go to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions, Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just one on the basis of Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and if I -- I'm seeking the co-operation of those who are assisting us, because we are ten minutes over time, but since you say it's only one question, that perhaps may convince everyone that it should be allowed. It is allowed. Further further cross-examination by Mr. Traldi:

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In response to the President's question, sir, you testified that an Official Note would be made after an interview. Was an Official Note made and sent up the chain regardless of whether the person being interviewed was found to be someone there was reason to detain?

utterances.speaker: MISO RODIC
utterances.text: Every person I saw and who was interviewed had an Official Note drawn up. However, I find your question imprecise. All I can say is that all those who were interrogated in terms of intelligence -- well, we drafted Official Notes in each case and we sent those notes up both lines of command; that is to say, to the corps, in terms of the intelligence and security chain, as well as up the chain of command of the 43rd Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's all I had, and I appreciate the Court's and everyone else's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, no questions arising from the questions from the Bench and Mr. Traldi's question. Mr. Rodic, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to the location of the videolink and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, and I want you -- wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can disconnect the videolink. And we thank you Madam Registrar at the location of the videolink for her assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we resume on Monday, the 16th of March, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
